title: Text as bytes
objectives: Encode text as UTF-8 bytes and explain why a tokeniser starts from bytes.

screens.title: How long is it?
screens.prose: A model never sees letters. It sees numbers, and the way text becomes numbers decides how long the input is. Take the price tag `Price £5`.

state.caption: Eight characters; the box is a space.

screens.question: `len('Price £5')` is 8. How many bytes does `'Price £5'.encode('utf-8')` hold?

options.why: You counted characters. The pound sign needs more than one byte.
You gave every character two bytes, as UTF-16 does. UTF-8 spends one byte on each plain letter.
The tokeniser sets a third length, the number of tokens. The bytes are fixed by UTF-8 before any tokeniser runs.

hints.text: Plain English letters, digits and spaces take one byte each.
The odd one out is the pound sign.
Seven characters take one byte each and `£` takes two: $7 + 2 = 9$.

feedback.correct: Nine bytes: one for each of the seven plain characters and two for `£`.
feedback.generic: Not yet. Count bytes, not characters, and look hard at the pound sign.

explain.text: Seven plain characters take one byte each and `£` takes two, so 9 bytes. A tokeniser later groups bytes into tokens: a third count we cannot know yet.

screens.title: Bytes under the characters
screens.prose: Each cell is one byte in hexadecimal, with its character above the byte that starts it. Bands mark characters that take more than one byte. Slide through four strings.

frames.caption: Up and the chart emoji: 4 characters, 7 bytes.

screens.question: How many bytes does the chart emoji take?

options.why: One byte covers only the first 128 characters: plain English letters, digits and punctuation.
Two bytes is what `£` and `é` take. Slide to the last string and count the band.
Three bytes is what `€` and `日` take. The emoji's band is one byte wider.

hints.text: Slide to the last string.
Count the cells under the emoji's band.

feedback.correct: Four bytes. Plain letters take 1, `£` and `é` take 2, `€` and `日` take 3, the emoji takes 4.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Slide to the last string and count the cells in its band.

explain.text: UTF-8 is a variable-length code: 1 byte for plain English, 2 for accented Latin, Greek, Cyrillic, Hebrew and Arabic, 3 for Chinese, Japanese and most other scripts, 4 for emoji. That is why bytes and characters disagree.

screens.title: Code points and UTF-8
screens.prose: Every character has a number, its **code point**: `ord('£')` is 163, written U+00A3. **UTF-8** stores a code point in 1 to 4 bytes. The first byte's leading bits say how many bytes follow, as the table shows.

state.caption: Every later byte of a character has the form `10xxxxxx` and carries 6 bits.

screens.question: `ord('€')` is 8364, which is U+20AC. How many bytes does UTF-8 use for it?

hints.text: Find the first row whose limit is at least U+20AC.
U+20AC is above U+07FF and below U+FFFF.
It falls in the third row: 3 bytes, carrying 16 bits.

feedback.correct: Three bytes. U+20AC lies between U+0800 and U+FFFF.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Compare U+20AC with the limits in the first column.

byKey.two: 8364 fits in 16 bits, and 16 bits fit in two bytes, but UTF-8 spends some bits on markers. A two-byte form carries only 11 bits, up to U+07FF.
byKey.four: Four bytes start at U+10000. U+20AC is far below that.

explain.text: U+20AC is above U+07FF, the most two bytes can carry, and below U+FFFF. So UTF-8 uses 3 bytes: `e2 82 ac`.

screens.title: Encode the pound sign by hand
screens.prose: 163 in binary is `10100011`. A two-byte form carries 11 bits, so pad it to `00010100011`. The first 5 bits go into `110xxxxx` and the last 6 into `10xxxxxx`.
screens.question: Fill in both bytes in hexadecimal.

hints.text: Join the marker and the bits, then read each group of four bits as one hexadecimal digit.
The first byte is `1100 0010`: `1100` is c and `0010` is 2.
The first byte is `1100 0010`, c2; the second is `1010 0011`, a3.

feedback.correct: `£` is `c2 a3`, exactly what Python's encoder gives.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Split each byte into two groups of four bits and read each as a hex digit.

byKey.swapped: You swapped the bytes. The first byte is the one that starts with `110`.
byKey.swapped-2: You swapped the bytes. The second byte is the one that starts with `10`.
byKey.decimal: 194 is the right byte written in decimal. Write it in hexadecimal: c2.
byKey.decimal-2: 163 is the right byte written in decimal. Write it in hexadecimal: a3.

explain.text: `11000010` is c2 and `10100011` is a3. The second byte happens to equal 163, because 163 lies between 128 and 191, so its bits already have the form `10xxxxxx`; for `é` (233) it would not.

screens.title: Where characters start
screens.prose: Here are the 12 bytes of `naïve café`. A byte of the form `10xxxxxx`, from 80 to bf in hex, only continues a character. Every other byte starts one.

state.caption: The bytes of naïve café, in hexadecimal.

screens.question: Tap every byte that starts a new character.

hints.text: Look for the bytes between 80 and bf.
There are two of them.
`af` and `a9` continue the characters started by `c3`. Tap the other ten.

feedback.correct: Ten starts, so ten characters, in twelve bytes.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Leave out the bytes between 80 and bf; tap all the others.

byKey.every-byte: You tapped all twelve. Two of them, `af` and `a9`, only continue the character before them.
byKey.c3: `af` lies between 80 and bf, so it continues the `ï` that `c3` started.
byKey.c11: `a9` lies between 80 and bf, so it continues the `é` that `c3` started.

explain.text: `c3 af` is `ï` and `c3 a9` is `é`; every other byte is a whole plain character. A decoder finds where characters start this way, from any position.

state.caption: Every later byte of a character has the form `10xxxxxx` and carries 6 bits.

Compare `ord(ch)` with `0x80`, `0x800` and `0x10000`.

screens.title: Each character's bytes
screens.prose: Write `char_spans(s)`: a list with one `(start, end)` pair per character, giving its bytes in `s.encode('utf-8')` with `end` excluded, as in a slice. For `£5` it is `[(0, 2), (2, 3)]`.

state.caption: naïve café: the bands are spans (2, 4) and (10, 12).

screens.question: Write `char_spans(s)`.

widget.solution:
def char_spans(s):
    spans, pos = [], 0
    for ch in s:
        cp = ord(ch)
        n = 1 if cp < 0x80 else 2 if cp < 0x800 else 3 if cp < 0x10000 else 4
        spans.append((pos, pos + n))
        pos += n
    return spans

tests.call: [b[a:e].decode('utf-8') for a, e in char_spans(s)] == list(s)

widget.how: Check runs 8 hidden tests. Each span is `(start, end)` with `end` excluded, as in a slice; the last test decodes every span of a mixed string back to its own character.

mutants.source:
def char_spans(s):
    return [(i, i + 1) for i in range(len(s))]
mutants.symptom: Gives character positions, not byte positions.

mutants.source:

    for ch in s:

def char_spans(s):
    spans, pos = [], 0
    for ch in s:
        cp = ord(ch)
        n = 1 if cp < 0x80 else 2 if cp < 0x800 else 3
        spans.append((pos, pos + n))

hints.text: Keep a running byte position.
Each character's span starts where the last one ended.
For each character, find its byte count `n`, append `(pos, pos + n)`, then add `n` to `pos`.

feedback.correct: Every span slices out exactly its own character.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-3: Test 3 checks the spans around `ï`. A two-byte character must move the position on by 2.
byKey.test-6: Test 6 has an emoji, which takes 4 bytes. Check your top row.

explain.text: The spans tile the bytes with no gap: each starts where the last ended. They are what a safe cut needs: cut only at a span's edge.

screens.title: A length check that lies
screens.prose: A data feed stores client names in a field of 10 bytes. The loader checks `len(name) <= 10` before writing.
screens.question: Which name passes the check but overflows the field?

options.why: Plain English, so its 10 characters are 10 bytes: it fits exactly.
It is 9 bytes, still within 10.
`len` gives 16, so the check already turns it away.

hints.text: `len` counts characters. The field counts bytes.
Which names have characters outside plain English?
`naïve café` is 10 characters, but `ï` and `é` take 2 bytes each: 12 bytes.

feedback.correct: It passes with `len` 10 but needs 12 bytes, so two bytes are cut off.
feedback.generic: Not quite. For each name, count bytes, not characters.

byKey.lloyds: `Lloyds plc` fills the field exactly: plain letters are one byte each, so its 10 characters are 10 bytes.
byKey.price: You found the £ and its extra byte, but 9 bytes still fit in 10.

explain.text: `len` counts characters, and the field counts bytes. `naïve café` has two two-byte characters, so 10 characters are 12 bytes. Check `len(name.encode('utf-8'))` instead.

screens.title: Cutting through a character
screens.prose: The feed cut `café` to its first 4 bytes: `b'caf\xc3'`. The byte `c3` starts a two-byte character whose second byte was lost. Plain `.decode('utf-8')` raises `UnicodeDecodeError`.
screens.question: What does `b'caf\xc3'.decode('utf-8', errors='replace')` return?

options.why: That is what `errors='ignore'` gives. `replace` keeps a marker where the broken character was.
The second byte of `é` is gone, so the decoder cannot rebuild it.
That is plain `.decode`. With `errors='replace'` it does not raise.

hints.text: `replace` swaps a broken sequence for one special character.
That character is U+FFFD, the replacement character.
The three whole characters decode, and `c3` becomes `\ufffd`.

feedback.correct: The broken byte becomes U+FFFD, the replacement character.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Think about what `replace`, as opposed to `ignore`, puts in place of the broken byte.

explain.text: Cutting bytes inside a character leaves a start byte with no ending. `errors='replace'` turns it into U+FFFD, so the damage shows; cut at a span's edge to avoid it.

screens.title: Why tokenisers start from bytes
screens.prose:
A character's byte count follows from its code point $c$:
$$\text{bytes}(c) = \begin{cases} 1 & c < 2^{7} \\ 2 & c < 2^{11} \\ 3 & c < 2^{16} \\ 4 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$
Every string, in any language, becomes bytes from 0 to 255. `makemore` used 27 characters; a byte-level tokeniser starts from 256 bytes.
screens.question: Why does a vocabulary of the 256 bytes never meet an unknown character?

options.text: Every character's UTF-8 encoding is made only of bytes 0 to 255
Unknown characters are too rare to matter in training
options.why: Rare is not never. A name, a ticker or an emoji turns up in real text; bytes cover it anyway.

options.text: UTF-8 turns every character into plain English letters
options.why: Only code points below 128 become one plain byte. The rest become 2 to 4 bytes from 128 to 255.

options.text: The tokeniser deletes characters it has not seen
options.why: Nothing is deleted. Each unseen character is spelt out as its bytes.

hints.text: What is every UTF-8 encoding made of?

feedback.correct: Any string encodes to bytes, and there are only 256 bytes, so nothing falls outside the vocabulary.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Think about what UTF-8 turns every string into.

explain.text: A character vocabulary of 27 or 65 symbols fails on the first character it lacks. Bytes cannot run out: every string is a list of numbers from 0 to 255.

screens.prose: A broker's order feed has a fixed field for the client's name. Write `safe_truncate(s, n_bytes)`: the longest start of `s` whose UTF-8 encoding fits in `n_bytes` bytes, never cutting through a character.

state.caption: At 7 bytes `Price £5` becomes `Price `: the £ will not fit whole.

screens.question: Write `safe_truncate(s, n_bytes)`, returning a string.

mutants.symptom: Cuts through a character and leaves U+FFFD.

hints.text: Add whole characters while they fit.
A character fits when the bytes used so far plus its own bytes are at most `n_bytes`.
Loop over `s`, add `len(ch.encode('utf-8'))` to a running total, and stop before the total would pass `n_bytes`.

feedback.correct: Every name fits its field and no character is split.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-2: Test 2 asks for 8 bytes of `Price £5`. `s[:8]` is 8 characters, which is 9 bytes here: count bytes.
byKey.test-6: Test 6 cuts `Société Générale` at 12 bytes. The second `é` would end at byte 13, so stop before it.

explain.text: Adding whole characters while they fit never splits one. `s.encode()[:n].decode('utf-8', errors='ignore')` also works: it drops the broken tail.

ideas: UTF-8 writes each code point in 1 to 4 bytes; the first byte's leading bits say how many, and later bytes start `10`.
Plain English is one byte per character, so its character and byte counts agree; `£` and `é` take 2, `€` 3 and emoji 4.
Every string becomes bytes from 0 to 255, so a byte-level tokeniser never meets an unknown character.
summary.trap: `len(s)` counts characters, not bytes; cutting bytes inside a character leaves a broken sequence.

quiz.prose: The course's data file holds the first 250,000 characters of Tiny Shakespeare. Every character in it is plain English: letters, digits, punctuation, spaces and newlines.
quiz.question: How many bytes does the file take in UTF-8?

feedback.correct: 250,000 bytes: plain English is one byte per character, so the two counts agree.
feedback.generic: Not quite. How many bytes does a plain English character take?

byKey.two-each: You gave every character two bytes. Characters below U+0080 take one byte each.

explain.text: Every character is below U+0080, so each takes one byte. For plain English text the character and byte counts are both 250,000.

quiz.question: How many bytes is the string `€5` in UTF-8?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Find each character's row in the UTF-8 table.

byKey.chars: That is the number of characters. `€` alone takes 3 bytes.
byKey.two-byte: You gave `€` two bytes. U+20AC is above U+07FF, so it takes 3.

explain.text: `€` is U+20AC, in the three-byte row, and `5` is plain, one byte. So `€5` is 4 bytes.

quiz.prose: A provider prices its model per token. Its tokeniser groups bytes that were common in its mostly English training text. A client sends the same report in English and in Greek, whose letters take 2 bytes each.
quiz.question: Why does the Greek report cost more?

options.text: More bytes, and fewer learned byte groups, so more tokens

options.why: The character counts are close. The cost comes from bytes and from which groups the tokeniser learned.

options.text: Providers charge a higher rate per token for other languages
options.why: The price per token is the same. The number of tokens is what differs.

options.text: Greek letters are unknown to the model and are sent twice
options.why: Nothing is unknown to a byte-level tokeniser; each letter is two bytes, which may each be a token.

feedback.correct: More bytes, and fewer learned groups, mean more tokens for the same meaning.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Think about bytes per character and which byte groups the tokeniser learned.

explain.text: Each Greek letter is 2 bytes, and the tokeniser learned few Greek groups. The same meaning becomes more tokens, so it costs more.

quiz.question: A decoder lands on the byte `9f` in the middle of a file. What can it tell?

options.text: It continues a character that started earlier

options.why: Two-byte characters start with `110xxxxx`, c0 to df. `9f` is `10011111`.

options.text: It is a plain English character
options.why: Plain characters are below 80. `9f` is above.

options.text: Nothing, without reading from the start of the file
options.why: The leading bits say it all: `10xxxxxx` always continues a character.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Write `9f` in binary and read its leading bits.

explain.text: `9f` is `10011111`, which starts `10`: a continuation byte. Every UTF-8 byte says whether it starts or continues a character.
